summary: Weekly POC sync focused on latency tuning. Reviewed TTFT and streaming adjustments, kernel selection anomalies for long sequences, and next steps for end-to-end benchmarks. Agreed to additional traces and an on-prem dry run.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2028-07-12
Time: 15:00 - 15:45 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood Solutions), Raj (Ember Head of AI), Sophie (Platform Eng), Tom (SRE)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um quick agenda, run through the latest bench results, dig into TTFT and streaming, kernel choices on longer sequences, then actions
[00:15] Raj: yep thanks, excited to see numbers we ran the batch overnight
[00:30] Liam: cool, quick context — we switched from the 8-bit quant profile to the new q4_0 variant and enabled streaming with prefix caching on the test cluster
[00:45] Sophie: small note — our real traffic has a lot of short queries but a 5% tail of 5k tokens for transcripts
[01:10] Priya: that tail really messes with batching and kernel selection, we saw some spike in 95th
[01:35] Liam: right, on the kernel side the runtime chose the generic matmul kernel for >2048 sequence lengths which increased op latency, we want to force the longer-seq kernel path
[02:00] Tom: can you remind us what you mean by TTFT here? we've been focused on p99 for end-to-end
[02:20] Maya: TTFT is time-to-first-token, it's critical for user perceived latency especially with streaming UIs
[02:40] Raj: our product target is TTFT < 300ms for short prompts, p99 < 1.2s for most interactions, tail handles transcripts
[03:10] Liam: the overnight run numbers — median TTFT 210ms with streaming, but p95 jumped to 1.4s when the 5% long sequences hit shared batchers
[03:35] Sophie: that's what we saw in prod traces too, the shared batcher queues up a long sequence and delays small ones
[04:00] Priya: options are: isolated pool for long sequences, or implement sequence-length-aware routing, or configure the runtime to limit batch lengths
[04:25] Liam: we demoed sequence-length-aware routing last week — it routes anything >1024 tokens to a Dedicated long-seq pool, that dropped small-query TTFT but costs more
[04:50] Raj: cost is a concern — can we do kernel-level tuning instead of separate pools? like select a kernel that handles both well
[05:10] Liam: it's tricky: longer sequences hit different memory paths, some kernels are optimized for attention with tiled matmul, others for short sequences with fused attention, switching incurs compiles
[05:35] Tom: how much compile time? if we switch kernels often is there a jitter impact
[05:55] Liam: compile/priming can be tens of ms to a few hundred ms on cold; that's why caching compiled kernels and warm pools matters
[06:20] Maya: another lever is streaming chunk size — smaller chunks reduce TTFT but increase token overhead; you saw token-perf tradeoff, right
[06:40] Sophie: yes, with chunked streaming set to 32 tokens we got TTFT down to ~150ms but token throughput dropped 8%
[07:00] Priya: also perf profiling showed KV cache hits are high for repeated prompts, but when sequences vary the cache become less effective
[07:25] Liam: we have two plans to try this week: 1) force kernel selection for sequences > 2048 to long-seq kernel and run benchmarks; 2) test sequence-aware routing to a long-seq Dedicated pool with streaming enabled
[07:50] Raj: for plan 2 what's the estimated unit cost uplift
[08:10] Maya: rough estimate 12–18% uplift at current qps for reserving a single long-seq instance, but TTFT and user experience improved significantly
[08:35] Tom: do you have perf traces we can look at? the traces from last night are in our logs but we need more detailed runtime traces
[08:55] Liam: yes I'll upload the kernel-selection and runtime traces, includes timeline of compile events, cache evictions
[09:15] Sophie: can we also get the exact quant profile used and the model variant, we saw a difference between q4_0 and q4_k_m that affected matmul patterns
[09:40] Liam: we used q4_0 on the test cluster; q4_k_m might be worth trying but it increased p95 in an earlier run
[10:00] Priya: curious about fallback policies — if a long seq is routed and pool is saturated, does it fallback to hosted or degrade to a smaller model
[10:25] Maya: Redwood has automatic fallback — policy can fall back to a compatible smaller variant or a hosted elastic pool, with a configurable cost/latency tradeoff
[10:45] Raj: policy would need to preserve data residency — can't go to hosted for certain transcripts
[11:05] Maya: noted, we can mark those requests as 'no-hosted-fallback' and only allow Dedicated/Private paths
[11:25] Tom: for the on-prem dry-run — network latency matters; if your control plane is cloud-managed how much chatter is there
[11:45] Liam: control plane calls are minimal after bootstrap; the inference path is entirely customer-local in Private deployments but logs/artifacts can be shipped or kept local
[12:05] Sophie: security docs please — SOC2 + KMS integration details are what our security team wants to see
[12:25] Maya: we'll share the security pack and on-prem architecture diagram
[12:45] Raj: ok let's go through the bench numbers in the shared sheet — column A is short prompts, B is long transcripts
[13:05] Liam: reading off numbers — short prompt median 180ms TTFT with streaming, p95 350ms, p99 720ms; long transcripts median token-latency 14ms/token but end-to-end p95 increases due to batching
[13:35] Sophie: those p99s are higher than we expected, can you break down time spent in kernel vs IO vs scheduling
[13:55] Liam: yes kernel ops account for ~55% of extra time on long sequences; scheduling and batching add ~30%, IO ~15%
[14:15] Tom: was prefetching of KV cache enabled on the long-seq kernel
[14:35] Liam: partial, we didn't enable aggressive prefetch because it increased memory pressure on 80GB cards
[14:55] Priya: speaking of hardware, what's the config of the Dedicated long-seq pool you're proposing
[15:15] Maya: we're proposing 2x 80GB A100 or equivalent per long-seq pool node, with autoscale burst to 3 nodes during peaks
[15:35] Raj: can we benchmark on GPUs we run on-prem? we have H100s and some 80GB A100s
[15:55] Liam: yes kernel selection differs across hardware, we'll include H100 traces; compiler chooses different kernel variants there
[16:15] Sophie: do you have a recommended sequence cutoff for routing? 1024 or 2048
[16:35] Liam: 1024 is a conservative cutoff; 2048 catches more but increases Dedicated cost — we should derive cutoff from Ember's seq-length histogram
[16:55] Priya: action for us to share that histogram today
[17:15] Raj: one more question — streaming chunking vs TTFT thresholds: is there a sweet spot for chunk size at our latency targets
[17:35] Liam: often 24–32 tokens for short prompts hits TTFT target but if prompts are token-dense we might go to 16; we'll run sensitivity tests
[17:55] Tom: what about priming/compile warm-up — can you pre-warm kernels for expected prompt prefixes
[18:15] Liam: yes using synthetic warmup and sample prompt prefixes helps; we can populate the cache during low-traffic hours
[18:35] Maya: ok let's capture concrete next steps — we'll run the forced-kernel and the sequence-aware routing benchmarks, upload traces, and schedule the on-prem dry-run
[18:55] Raj: sounds good
[19:10] Sophie: one more ask — can you include cost delta scenarios in the quote, like 1 node vs 2 node long-seq pools
[19:30] Maya: yes will include cost scenarios
[19:45] Priya: any concerns about model accuracy/regression with quant changes
[20:05] Liam: we ran a small evaluation and didn't see significant regression between q4_0 and q4_k_m for your prompt set, but we'll run a larger eval
[20:25] Tom: timeline — when do you expect results
[20:40] Maya: we'll aim to have initial benchmark runs and traces up by 2028-07-13 and draft pricing by 2028-07-14
[21:00] Raj: ok wrap up
[21:15] Maya: recap next steps and action items, thanks everyone

End transcript
